title: Problem Overview: Composites Dividing n! + 1
content: By **Wilson's theorem**, every prime p divides (p-1)! + 1. Erdos asked: how many **composite** numbers share this property? Let A(x) count composites u < x such that u | n! + 1 for some n. The conjecture is that A(x) <= x^{o(1)}, meaning composites dividing some factorial-plus-one are extremely rare.
mathContext: This problem connects **factorial arithmetic** with **primality testing** and the distribution of composites. Wilson's theorem provides a complete characterization for primes: p | (p-1)! + 1 iff p is prime. The question of which composites also divide some n! + 1 probes the boundary between primes and composites in modular arithmetic. Known examples (25, 121, 169, 437) are all **prime powers** or products of nearby primes, suggesting a deep structural constraint.

title: Factorial Plus One Divisibility
content: **DividesFactorialPlusOne u** holds when there exists a natural number n such that u | n! + 1. This is the core predicate: asking whether u appears as a factor of some shifted factorial.
mathContext: For primes, Wilson's theorem guarantees n = p - 1 always works. For composites, the existence of such an n is not guaranteed and is the central mystery of this problem. The predicate is existential -- we only need one witness n, regardless of how large it is.

title: Composite Counting Function A(x)
content: **factorialCompositeCount x** counts the composites u < x (with u >= 2 and u not prime) satisfying DividesFactorialPlusOne u. Uses Set.ncard for the cardinality of the composite factorial set.
mathContext: The counting function A(x) is the quantitative heart of the problem. The conjecture A(x) <= x^{o(1)} means A(x) grows slower than any power of x -- equivalently, for every epsilon > 0, A(x) <= x^epsilon for large x. This would make the composite factorial set extremely sparse among all composites.

title: Main Conjecture (OPEN)
content: **ErdosProblem1073**: For every epsilon > 0, there exists N_0 such that A(x) <= x^epsilon for all x >= N_0. Equivalently, A(x) = x^{o(1)}. This remains **open** -- no upper bound better than trivial is known.
mathContext: The x^{o(1)} bound is extremely strong. Even proving A(x) = o(x) (sublinear growth) would be significant progress. The difficulty stems from our poor understanding of the **multiplicative structure** of n! + 1: factoring n! + 1 for large n is computationally intractable, and theoretical tools for controlling its divisors are limited.

title: Wilson's Theorem (Proved from Mathlib)
content: Every prime p divides (p-1)! + 1. This is **fully proved** using Mathlib's ZMod.wilsons_lemma: in Z/pZ, (p-1)! = -1, so (p-1)! + 1 = 0 mod p. The corollary **prime_divides_factorial_plus_one** wraps this into the DividesFactorialPlusOne predicate.
mathContext: Wilson's theorem is one of the earliest primality characterizations (proved by Lagrange in 1771). The Lean proof leverages Mathlib's algebraic infrastructure: working in **ZMod p** where p is prime, (p-1)! = -1 follows from the fact that every nonzero element pairs with its multiplicative inverse, except for the self-inverse elements 1 and -1.

title: Composite Witness: 25 | 4! + 1
content: **25 divides 4! + 1 = 25**, verified by native_decide. This is the smallest composite satisfying DividesFactorialPlusOne. Note 25 = 5^2 and 4 = 5 - 1, so this mirrors Wilson's theorem for p = 5.
mathContext: The fact that 25 = 5^2 divides 4! + 1 = (5-1)! + 1 is not a coincidence: by Wilson's theorem, 5 | 4! + 1. Since 4! + 1 = 25 = 5^2, the prime square also divides. This pattern of **prime-square divisibility** appears again with 121 = 11^2 | 5! + 1 and 169 = 13^2 | 12! + 1.

title: Composite Witness: 437 | 18! + 1
content: **437 = 19 * 23** divides 18! + 1, verified by native_decide. Unlike the prime-square examples, 437 is a product of **two distinct primes**. Note 18 = 19 - 1, connecting to Wilson's theorem for p = 19.
mathContext: Since 19 | (18)! + 1 by Wilson's theorem, we need 23 | 18! + 1 as well. This is a numerical coincidence: 23 does not divide 22! + 1 via Wilson's pattern, but happens to divide 18! + 1. Such coincidences make the problem difficult -- there is no structural reason forcing 23 to cooperate.

title: Coprimality Lemma
content: If u >= 2 and u | n! + 1, then **gcd(u, n!) = 1**. Proof: any common divisor of u and n! would also divide n! + 1 - n! = 1. This is a clean application of the Bezout-style argument that consecutive values are coprime.
mathContext: This coprimality is the key structural constraint on composites dividing n! + 1. It immediately implies that **all prime factors of u must exceed n** (otherwise they would appear in n! and violate coprimality). This severely limits which composites can divide n! + 1 for a given n.

title: Prime Factors Must Exceed n
content: If u | n! + 1 with u >= 2, then **every prime factor p of u satisfies p > n**. This is proved by contradiction: if p <= n and p is prime, then p | n!, contradicting gcd(u, n!) = 1.
mathContext: This theorem is the formalization's most important structural result. It means that if composite u = p * q divides n! + 1, then both p and q exceed n, forcing u > n^2. For u < x, this means n < sqrt(x), providing an indirect bound on which n values can witness u's membership in the factorial set.

title: Four Known Composites Below 500
content: The four known small composites -- **25, 121, 169, 437** -- are all verified members of compositeFactorialSet 500. Each membership proof combines the computational witness, non-primality (by decide), and the bound u < 500.
mathContext: These four values are the complete list of known composites below 500 satisfying the divisibility condition. The scarcity (4 out of roughly 400 composites below 500) is consistent with the conjecture that A(x) = x^{o(1)}. Finding additional examples requires checking divisibility of n! + 1 by each composite, which is computationally expensive for large n.
